format: html

```{r}
#| warning: false
# Load packages
library(survival)
library(ggsurvfit)
library(survminer)
```


## Problem 1

This problem uses data from a placebo-controlled clinical trial of
D-penicillamine (DPCA) for primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC).
PBC destroys bile ducts in the liver, causing bile to accumulate,
which causes progressive tissue damage and ultimately leads to liver failure.
The outcome in this study is time to death.
I'm not sure what the time origin is.
The data set and codebook are available in the GitHub repository.

```{r}
# Load data
pbc <- read.csv("pbc.csv")
```

### Part (a)

Create a single plot with two Kaplan-Meier curves on it,
one for the DPCA group and one for the placebo group.

```{r}
# Create integer-valued status variable
sum(is.na(pbc$status))
pbc$status_int <- 0
pbc$status_int[pbc$status == "Dead"] <- 1

# Kaplan-Meier curves
ggsurvfit(survfit2(Surv(time = years,
                        event = status_int) ~ rx,
                   data = pbc)) +
  labs(x = "Years",
       y = "Probability of Survival") +
  add_risktable()
```

### Part (b)

Run a Cox regression with `rx` as the only explanatory variable.
Then, check whether the proportional hazards assumption is met.
If it is, interpret the coefficients. If it isn't, move on to the next problem.

```{r}
# Ensure "Placebo" is the reference group
pbc$rx <- as.factor(pbc$rx)
pbc$rx <- relevel(x = pbc$rx,
                  ref = "Placebo")

# Cox regresssion
mod_01 <- coxph(formula = Surv(time = years,
                               event = status_int) ~ rx,
                data = pbc)

# Complementary log-log plot
ggsurvplot(fit = survfit(Surv(time = years,
                              event = status_int) ~ rx,
                         data = pbc),
           fun = "cloglog")

# Schoenfeld residual test
ggcoxzph(cox.zph(mod_01))
```

The lines in the complementary log-log plot cross multiple times.
The Schoenfeld residual test is not significant,
but the Schoenfeld residual plot shows a non-flat line.
I'm not convinced that the proportional hazards assumption is met,
so I'm not going to interpret the coefficients.

### Part (c)

Run a Cox regression with at least two explanatory variables.
One of the explanatory variables must be `rx`,
and you must include at least one interaction.
Then, check whether the proportional hazards assumption is met.
If it is, interpret the coefficients. If it isn't, move on to the next problem.

```{r}
# Create character variable for sex
sum(is.na(pbc$sex))
pbc$sex_ch <- "Male"
pbc$sex_ch[pbc$sex == 1] <- "Female"

# Cox regresssion
mod_02 <- coxph(formula = Surv(time = years,
                               event = status_int) ~ rx * sex_ch + age,
                data = pbc)

# Schoenfeld residual test
ggcoxzph(cox.zph(mod_02))

# Results
summary(mod_02)

# Interaction terms
exp(sum(mod_02$coefficients[c(1,4)]))
exp(sum(mod_02$coefficients[c(2,4)]))
```


The Schoenfeld residual plots still don't look flat,
even though the tests are not significant.
I'm going to provide interpretations for the coefficients,
just so people can get practice interpreting coefficients:

- $\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_1\right) = 1.206100$:
At a given time $t$,
women on DPCA have a 21% higher hazard rate than women on placebo,
holding age constant.
- $\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_2\right) = 1.905265$:
At a given time $t$,
men on placebo have a 90% higher hazard rate than women on placebo,
holdling age constant.
- $\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_1+\hat{\beta}_4\right) = 0.5974903$:
At a given time $t$,
men on DPCA have a 40% lower hazard rate than men on placebo,
holding age constant.
- $\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_2+\hat{\beta}_4\right) = 0.9438501$:
At a given time $t$,
men on DPCA have a 6% lower hazard rate than women on DPCA,
holding age constant.
- $\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_3\right) = 1.040865$:
At a given time $t$,
a person who is $x + 1$ years old has a 4% higher hazard rate
than a person who is $x$ years old,
holding treatment group and sex constant.



### Part (d)

Is there evidence of effect modification in your analysis?
Justify your answer.

The p-value for the interaction term is non-significant,
so you could argue that there is no evidence of effect modification.
However, the effect of DPCA is in opposite directions for men and women,
so you could also argue that that's clinically meaningful.

Just out of curiosity, I'm going to make some new
Kaplan-Meier curves for each combination of sex and treatment status.

```{r}
# Kaplan-Meier curves
ggsurvfit(survfit2(Surv(time = years,
                        event = status_int) ~ rx + sex_ch,
                   data = pbc)) +
  labs(x = "Years",
       y = "Probability of Survival")
```

Within sex, the survival curves for DPCA and placebo cross.
I'm not convinced there's an effect of treatment, even when stratified
by sex, and I'm not convinced that the effect of treatment is different
across sex.

## Problem 2

This problem uses data from a study of time to death after a kidney transplant.
The data set and documentation are available in the GitHub repository.

```{r}
# Load data
kidney <- read.csv("kidney_data.csv")
```

Create a Cox regression model, check the assumption of proportional hazards,
and interpret the coefficients.

```{r}
# Create character variables for gender and race
kidney$gender_ch <- as.character(NA)
kidney$gender_ch[kidney$gender == 1] <- "Male"
kidney$gender_ch[kidney$gender == 2] <- "Female"
kidney$race_ch <- as.character(NA)
kidney$race_ch[kidney$race == 1] <- "White"
kidney$race_ch[kidney$race == 2] <- "Black"

# Cox regresssion
mod_03 <- coxph(formula = Surv(time = obstime,
                               event = death) ~ gender_ch + race_ch + age,
                data = kidney)

# Schoenfeld residual test
ggcoxzph(cox.zph(mod_03))

# Results
summary(mod_03)
```


The Schoenfeld residual test is non-significant for every covariate,
and the curves are flat,
so the proportional hazards assumption is met.

- $\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_1\right) = 0.973810$:
At a given time $t$,
the hazard rate for males is 3% lower than the hazard rate for females,
holding race and age constant.
- $\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_2\right) = 0.8902$:
At a given time $t$,
the hazard rate for white people is 11% lower than the hazard rate
for Black people, holding gender and age constant.
- $\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_3\right) = 1.0524$:
At a given time $t$,
each additional year of age is associated with a 5% higher hazard rate,
holding gender and race constant.
